questions.question: Describe where the wettest and driest areas of the world are found on an annual rainfall map.
questions.expected_answer: The wettest areas, with more than two thousand millimetres a year, lie in a band near the equator, such as the Amazon Basin, the Congo Basin and the islands of Southeast Asia. The driest areas, with less than two hundred and fifty millimetres, lie roughly along the tropics, such as the Sahara, Arabian, Namib, Atacama and Australian deserts. Polar areas such as Antarctica are also very dry.

questions.question: Explain three reasons why some places are wet and others are dry.
questions.expected_answer: Near the equator, warm, moist air rises, cools and forms rain clouds, while near the tropics dry air sinks, so clouds cannot form. Mountains force moist air to rise and drop rain on the windward side, leaving a dry rain shadow on the leeward side. Cold ocean currents, such as the Benguela Current, cool the air so it forms fog instead of rain, and places far inland are often dry because the winds have lost their moisture.

questions.question: Describe the pattern of rainfall in South Africa and explain it.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa is a dry country, with rainfall well below the world average, and rainfall decreases from east to west. The east is wetter because moist winds from the warm Indian Ocean drop rain on the coast and the eastern slopes of the escarpment. The west is drier because the winds have lost their moisture by the time they cross the plateau, and the cold Benguela Current keeps the west coast dry. Cape Town is an exception, with winter rain from cold fronts.
